analysis.one_liner: Funds bigger student aid grants by rolling back parts of the 2017 estate tax and alternative minimum tax cuts.
analysis.headline: A bill to pay for expanded student aid by clawing back the 2017 estate tax and AMT giveaways never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Degrees Not Debt Act of 2018, introduced by Sen. Martin Heinrich, would have repealed two 2017 tax-law benefits that go overwhelmingly to wealthy families — the new larger estate and gift tax exemption and the alternative minimum tax exemption — and spent the resulting revenue on bigger need-based federal student aid. It also would have required colleges to report standard performance numbers, like net price, graduation, transfer-out, average debt, and default rates. The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on June 6, 2018, and nothing further ever happened to it: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no cosponsors, before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019. analysis.who_benefits: Low- and middle-income students and their families, who would receive more need-based federal student aid paid for by rolling back tax benefits that flow mainly to the wealthiest households. [S2] Students and families choosing colleges would also get standardized, comparable performance data — average net price broken into tuition, fees, and living costs, average debt at graduation, and default rates — instead of self-reported marketing figures. [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Needy college students and their families

how_it_helps.text: Increases need-based federal student aid to students at institutions of higher education, using revenue from repealing the 2017 alternative minimum tax exemption and the increased estate and gift tax exemption.

Requires each state receiving funds to report a standard set of key performance indicators for its colleges, including average net price by cost type, graduation and transfer-out rates, average student loan debt at time of completion, and default rates.

The tax provisions being repealed were enacted in 2017 and primarily benefit wealthy households and large estates, so the bill's cost falls on high-net-worth families rather than students or ordinary taxpayers.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy households and heirs of large estates, whose 2017 estate and gift tax exemption increase and alternative minimum tax exemption would be repealed to fund the aid. [S2] Colleges would also face new federal reporting requirements on prices, debt, and outcomes. [S3]

drawbacks.text: The bill would raise taxes on wealthy families by repealing the 2017 estate and gift tax exemption increase and the AMT exemption; supporters of the 2017 tax law argued those provisions reduce double taxation of family businesses and farms and that repealing them would discourage investment.

The performance-reporting regime could work against colleges that serve high-risk, low-income students: metrics like graduation and default rates can make an institution that takes a chance on struggling students look bad compared with one that selects only well-prepared applicants, and the bill's funding conditions are tied to those reports.
With zero cosponsors and no committee action, the bill offered no test of whether its tax-offset approach could attract the votes needed to become law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is simple and explicit: take back two 2017 tax benefits that go mainly to the wealthy and spend the money on need-based student aid. [S2] For a low- or middle-income student, the aid increase is a direct benefit. The honest costs are that heirs of large estates would pay more tax [S2], and tying funding and reporting to graduation, debt, and default metrics risks pressuring colleges to avoid enrolling harder-to-serve students. [S3] On the revenue side, repealing the AMT exemption and the estate tax increase is a broad-based way to raise money but is exactly the kind of offset that makes the bill a hard political sell in a Senate whose majority had just enacted those provisions.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and sent to the Senate Finance Committee on June 6, 2018, and the committee never acted on it before Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and it never got a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Sen. Martin Heinrich introduced the Degrees Not Debt Act of 2018 in the Senate on June 6, 2018.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which handles both tax law and student aid.
No further action was taken: the bill had zero cosponsors and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy households and heirs of large estates, who kept the 2017 estate tax and AMT exemptions because the bill never advanced; low-income students gained nothing because the aid increase never happened.

against.what_they_did: The bill, which would have rolled back 2017 tax-cut provisions passed the prior year, was never brought to the floor; it died with zero cosponsors from either party.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by one Democrat with zero cosponsors of either party and died in committee without a vote, in a Senate controlled by the party that had passed the 2017 tax provisions the bill would repeal. [S4] [S5]

industries.note: The bill's funding comes from repealing the 2017 estate and gift tax exemption increase and the AMT exemption, both of which primarily benefit high-net-worth families; the bill's death left these benefits fully in place. [S2]

The bill would channel increased federal need-based aid to institutions — money that flows through and supports the higher-education sector — while imposing new federal reporting duties on prices, graduation, debt, and default rates. The aid expansion entrenches institutions as the recipients of public support; the metrics pressure them to be transparent. [S2] [S3]
